en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,
Pācittiya Section
Chattupāhanavagga 95.
The Training Rule on Asking Questions.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, bhikkhunīs were asking questions of a bhikkhu who had not granted them the opportunity.
The bhikkhus complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these bhikkhunīs ask questions of a bhikkhu who has not granted them the opportunity? ... [as before] ...
“Is it true, monks, that nuns are asking questions of a monk who has not granted them the opportunity?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
“How indeed, bhikkhus, can bhikkhunīs ask a question of a bhikkhu who has not granted them the opportunity?
This, bhikkhus, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of those with faith...
And thus, bhikkhus, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:”
“Whichever nun, however, should ask a question of a monk who has not granted her leave, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whichever nun” means whichever one of whatever kind... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context. "Without having made an opportunity" means:
Without having asked for permission.
"A bhikkhunī" means one who is fully ordained.
"Should ask a question":
if, having requested an opportunity regarding the Suttanta, he asks about the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having requested an opportunity regarding the Vinaya, he asks about the Suttanta or the Abhidhamma, there is an offense of expiation.
If, having obtained permission regarding the Abhidhamma, one asks a question concerning the Suttanta or the Vinaya, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one has not asked for permission, yet perceives that permission has not been asked for, and one asks a question, there is an offense of expiation.
If one has not asked for permission, but is in doubt as to whether permission was asked for, and one asks a question, there is an offense of expiation.
If she has not asked for permission, but perceives that she has asked for permission, and asks a question, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she has asked for permission, but perceives that she has not asked for permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she has asked for permission, but is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she has asked for permission and perceives that she has asked for permission,
there is no offense.
There is no offense if she asks after having had permission granted.
If she has had a place designated without specifying it and asks anywhere,
or if she is insane,
or if she is a first-offender.
The twelfth training rule is concluded.
